# Status report: jf2 allocator test on kestrel

Date: 2026-11-20

## Short version

On the read-heavy benchmark, replacing jemalloc 5.3 with jf2 (our fork of that memory allocator) in kestrel (our key-value store) reduced p99 latency from 2140 microseconds (us) to 870 us, which is 59.3% lower. p99 latency is the level that 99% of requests stay under. Throughput and median latency did not change measurably, memory use rose by 5.7 GB (9.3%), and the write-heavy benchmark is not tested yet.

## Words used here

- **Build A**: commit 4f1c2aa of the main branch with jemalloc 5.3, the allocator kestrel uses today.
- **Build B**: the same commit with jf2.
- **YCSB**: Yahoo Cloud Serving Benchmark, a standard load test for key-value stores. Workload B is read-heavy and workload A is write-heavy.
- **p50, p99, p99.9 latency**: the latency that 50%, 99%, and 99.9% of requests stay under.
- **kops/s**: thousands of operations per second.
- **RSS**: resident set size, the physical memory that the process holds.
- **Decay purge**: the step in which jemalloc returns unused memory to the operating system.
- **Latency spike**: a short period in which requests take much longer than usual.

## Test setup

- **Host:** bench-07 (the test server), 2 x 32-core Xeon, 512 GB memory, kernel 6.8.
- **System load:** load average 0.4 before the runs, which is less than 1% of the 64 cores busy.
- **Workload:** YCSB-B, 64 client threads, 10 minutes per run.
- **Runs:** 5 per build, in alternating order (A, B, A, B, ...).

## Results

```
p99 and p99.9 latency, median of 5 runs (1 block = 250 us)

p99    A  █████████ 2140 us
       B  ███ 870 us  (59.3% lower than A)

p99.9  A  ███████████████████████████████████████ 9800 us
       B  ████████████ 3100 us  (68.4% lower than A)
```

Both high-percentile latencies fell by more than half with jf2.

Each value is the median of 5 runs, with the lowest and highest run in parentheses.

| Metric | Build A (jemalloc 5.3) | Build B (jf2) | Change, B against A |
|---|---|---|---|
| Throughput, kops/s | 412 (405 to 418) | 409 (401 to 415) | -3 kops/s (-0.7%) |
| p50 latency, us | 118 (116 to 121) | 119 (117 to 121) | +1 us (+0.8%) |
| p99 latency, us | 2140 (1890 to 2610) | 870 (820 to 940) | -1270 us (-59.3%) |
| p99.9 latency, us | 9800 (7200 to 14100) | 3100 (2700 to 3900) | -6700 us (-68.4%) |
| RSS at end of run, GB | 61.2 | 66.9 | +5.7 GB (+9.3%) |

## What the results show

- **p99 and p99.9 latency improved in every run.** The highest B run is below the lowest A run for both metrics: 940 us against 1890 us for p99, and 3900 us against 7200 us for p99.9 [Ref1].
- **Throughput and p50 latency show no measurable change.** The differences are 3 kops/s (0.7%) and 1 us (0.8%), and the run ranges of the two builds overlap [Ref1].
- **Memory use is higher with jf2.** RSS at the end of the run rose from 61.2 GB to 66.9 GB [Ref1].

## Cause of the spikes

- **Measured:** in build A, the spikes occur at the same time as the decay purge. perf (the Linux sampling profiler) placed 31% of the samples from the spike periods in je_arena_decay, the jemalloc function that runs the purge [Ref2].
- **Hypothesis:** jf2 removes the spikes because it runs the purge in a background thread, so request threads do not wait for it. A perf profile of build B that shows no je_arena_decay samples in request threads would confirm this.

## Replaced run

Run 3 of build B had a 40 s stall at minute 7. The stall was traced to logrotate (the nightly log rotation job, started by the cron scheduler), not to the allocator. The run was repeated, and the B results use the repeat in place of the original run [Ref3].

## Not tested

- YCSB-A (write-heavy).
- More than 64 client threads.
- NUMA pinning (binding threads and memory to one processor socket).

The results apply only to the read-heavy workload at 64 client threads without pinning.

## Open question

Is the RSS increase of 5.7 GB (9.3%) acceptable? The capacity team must approve it.

## Next steps

1. Run YCSB-A tomorrow (2026-11-21).
2. Ask the capacity team to decide on the RSS increase.
3. If the capacity team approves, enable jf2 in staging (the pre-production environment), controlled by a feature flag.

## References

- [Ref1] Results table above: 5 runs per build on bench-07, 2026-11-20.
- [Ref2] perf profile of build A during the spike periods, same test session.
- [Ref3] Investigation of the stall in run 3 of build B, same test session.

---

Gaps I could not fill from the notes:

- **RSS range:** the notes give one RSS value per build and no lowest-to-highest range, so the table has none.
- **Raw data locations:** the notes have no paths for the run logs or the perf profile, so the references name the runs only.
- **Build B profile:** the notes do not mention a perf profile of build B. If you have one, the hypothesis line can become a measured claim.
- **Build A configuration:** stock jemalloc 5.3 has a `background_thread` option that moves purging off application threads. The notes do not say whether build A had it enabled, and a reader may ask why the fork is needed.
- **Date of the next run:** 2026-11-21 is a Saturday. Change the date in step 1 if you meant the next working day.
